source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
Soil cover (mulching with crop residue) had a large measured effect on corn yield in an upland trial referenced in this source: yield increased by 61%, from about 2.83 t/ha without mulch to about 4.70 t/ha with mulch applied (roughly 3 tonnes/ha of straw spread over the field). The benefit is attributed to more favourable soil temperature and moisture conditions, and to reduced risk of early-wet-season establishment failure.

This yield response corresponds to a large increase in profitability -- from roughly $28-29/ha net profit without mulch to roughly $176-177/ha net profit with mulch, after accounting for the added cost of the mulch itself (see the mulching cost-benefit budget topic for the full itemised figures). Because the return was so much larger than the added cost, the source recommends mulching as a practice worth trying broadly where crop residue or straw is available, particularly for early-wet-season plantings where establishment risk is highest.
